body:
Devotion as a religious path

In medieval India, many religious teachers placed personal devotion, ethical conduct and inner commitment at the centre of spiritual life. Bhakti means devotion or loving participation in the divine. It developed in several Hindu religious traditions rather than as a single organisation with one founder. Sufism, known in Islamic writings as tasawwuf, developed within Islam and emphasised love of God, spiritual discipline and the guidance of experienced teachers.

Both traditions could appeal to people who found elaborate ritual or inherited religious privilege inadequate. Yet they were not identical faiths: Sufi teachings remained connected with Islam and its understanding of God, while bhakti took diverse forms associated with different deities and philosophical ideas.

Bhakti itself had different forms

A basic distinction is between saguna bhakti, devotion to a God understood with qualities or a recognisable form, and nirguna bhakti, devotion to a formless, attributeless Supreme Reality. These are categories of devotional belief, not two Sufi orders.

  • Saguna examples: The Tamil Alvars sang of Vishnu, the Nayanars of Shiva, and Mirabai of Krishna. The traditions of the Alvars and Nayanars grew especially from about the 6th to 9th centuries. There were 12 Alvars and 63 Nayanars.
  • Nirguna examples: Kabir criticised outward ritual and spoke of a formless Supreme God; Guru Nanak emphasised remembrance of the one, formless Divine. His teachings later became foundational to a distinct Sikh religious tradition.

Because these strands differed, it is inaccurate to say that all bhakti saints rejected images, temples or established worship. Some criticised such practices, while others actively supported temple devotion.

Why the traditions came into contact

From the 12th century onward, expanding towns, craft production, trade networks and the Delhi Sultanate brought more people into contact with teachers of varied backgrounds. Many devotional compositions used the spoken languages of artisans, peasants and other listeners. North Indian sants, Sufis and yogic groups sometimes discussed similar questions about devotion, social status and the search for God, although each retained distinctive teachings.

Prelims focus

  • Bhakti: personal devotion; Sufism: the mystical devotional tradition within Islam.
  • Alvars: Vishnu, 12 saints; Nayanars: Shiva, 63 saints.
  • Saguna: divine qualities or form; nirguna: formless Supreme Reality.
  • Kabir: a prominent nirguna saint; Mirabai: a Krishna devotee.
  • Trap: Criticism of ritual did not characterise every bhakti tradition or every Sufi.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – II, Class 7, Chapter 8, “Devotional Paths to the Divine,” printed pp. 104–107, 110–114, 116–119; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Class 12, Theme 6, “Bhakti-Sufi Traditions,” printed pp. 143–144, 147–149, 153.]

pictures.caption: Public singing made devotional ideas accessible beyond learned circles.

title: Devotion in Medieval India: Bhakti and Sufism

body:
What makes a silsila?

A silsila is a recognised chain of Sufi spiritual teachers and disciples. The chain was believed to transmit spiritual guidance and blessing across generations, ultimately linking the order to the Prophet Muhammad. Different silsilas followed distinct forms of training, called a tariqa (spiritual path or method).

  • Shaikh, pir or murshid: the spiritual master who instructs followers.
  • Murid: a disciple who accepts the master's guidance.
  • Khalifa: the designated spiritual successor authorised to continue the teaching; here it does not mean a ruler of an empire.

Orders were not always named after their Indian centres. Chishti derives from Chisht, a place in present-day Afghanistan; Qadiri is named after the teacher Abd al-Qadir Jilani.

The khanqah as a living institution

A khanqah was a Sufi hospice where a master and disciples lived, prayed, taught and received visitors. It could contain a communal hall, or jama'at khana, along with rooms and a kitchen. Its purpose went beyond lodging: visitors sought guidance, participated in worship or received food and shelter.

At prominent Chishti hospices, an open langar provided meals. Such kitchens could be supported by futuh, offerings freely given without being asked for. Individual hospices differed in how they acquired and used resources.

Practices: remembrance, music and pilgrimage

Zikr means remembrance or repetition of God's names. Sama means devotional listening, frequently involving music; qawwali is a form of Sufi devotional singing associated especially with Chishti practice. Music was important in some silsilas but was not a universal requirement of Sufism.

A dargah is the tomb-shrine of a deceased saint, unlike a khanqah, which is primarily the place where a living community gathers. Ziyarat means visiting a sacred shrine. Urs, commonly observed on a saint's death anniversary, commemorates the believed union of the saint's soul with God. A saint described as wali was revered as a friend of God; devotees sought the saint's barakat, or spiritual blessing.

Different attitudes to religious law

Ba-shari'a refers to Sufis who observed Islamic religious law, while be-shari'a refers to unconventional ascetics who deliberately departed from prescribed law or ritual. Some Qalandars and Malangs exemplified the latter pattern. This distinction describes a religious orientation; it should not be confused with the names Chishti, Suhrawardi, Qadiri or Naqshbandi.

Prelims focus

  • Silsila: spiritual teacher–disciple chain; tariqa: spiritual method.
  • Pir or murshid: teacher; murid: disciple; khalifa: designated successor.
  • Khanqah: hospice; dargah: tomb-shrine.
  • Zikr: remembrance; sama: devotional listening; ziyarat: pilgrimage.
  • Urs: a saint's death-anniversary observance.
  • Trap: Be-shari'a does not describe all Sufis.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Class 12, Theme 6, sections 6.1–6.2 and 7.1–7.2, printed pp. 153–157; NCERT, Our Pasts – II, Class 7, Chapter 8, printed pp. 110–112.]

pictures.alt: Teachers guide disciples; authorised khalifas continue the silsila and may establish khanqahs. A deceased wali may have a dargah visited at ziyarat and urs.
pictures.caption: Teaching continued through disciples, successors and linked hospices.

title: Sufi Silsilas, Spiritual Teachers and Khanqah Life

body:
How the Chishtis became influential

The Chishti silsila originated around Chisht in present-day Afghanistan and became particularly influential in the Indian subcontinent from the late 12th century. Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti established its famous Indian centre at Ajmer, Rajasthan. He is popularly remembered as Gharib Nawaz, or benefactor of the poor. Through a network of teachers and hospices, Chishti influence reached Delhi, Punjab and the Deccan.

Match each saint with the correct place

  • Muinuddin Chishti: Ajmer, Rajasthan; his dargah became a major pilgrimage centre.
  • Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki: Delhi; an important early Chishti teacher.
  • Fariduddin Ganj-i Shakar (Baba Farid): Ajodhan, now Pakpattan in Pakistan; verses associated with him were later included in Sikh scripture.
  • Nizamuddin Auliya: Ghiyaspur near Delhi; a major 14th-century Chishti master who died in 1325.
  • Nasiruddin Chiragh-i Dehli: Delhi; a later Chishti master who died in 1356.
  • Banda Nawaz Gesu Daraz: Gulbarga, Karnataka; associated with the movement's spread into the Deccan.

Food, gifts and distance from political office

Nizamuddin Auliya's khanqah at Ghiyaspur received poets, merchants, travellers, poor visitors, Hindu yogis and others. Its communal kitchen served food with the help of voluntary gifts. Chishti masters commonly valued simplicity and independence from rulers. They often accepted unrequested donations of money or goods and used them for food, clothing and the hospice, rather than accumulating wealth.

Independence did not mean no contact with rulers. Kings sought a saint's prestige and blessing, and Chishti shrines received royal gifts. In an account about Nizamuddin Auliya, the master declined a ruler's offer of landed property; this illustrates a preference rather than an absolute rule for every Chishti.

Music, language and Ajmer's pilgrimage traditions

The Chishtis used sama and devotional poetry to cultivate remembrance of God. Amir Khusrau, a disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya, is associated with the qaul, a hymn used in qawwali performance. Chishti circles used Persian and spoken languages such as Hindavi, allowing teaching and poetry to reach local audiences.

Ajmer's shrine drew visitors of different backgrounds. The Mughal emperor Akbar repeatedly visited it and offered a large cooking cauldron in 1568. The shrine also lay on a travel route linking Delhi and Gujarat, helping explain its wider reach.

Prelims focus

  • Muinuddin Chishti–Ajmer; title: Gharib Nawaz.
  • Baba Farid–Ajodhan/Pakpattan; Nizamuddin Auliya–Delhi.
  • Nasiruddin Chiragh-i Dehli–Delhi; Banda Nawaz Gesu Daraz–Gulbarga.
  • Nizamuddin Auliya: died 1325; Amir Khusrau: associated with the qaul.
  • Akbar: donated a cauldron at Ajmer in 1568.
  • Trap: Chishti distance from court office did not forbid all royal donations.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – II, Class 7, Chapter 8, printed p. 112; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Class 12, Theme 6, sections 7.1–7.4, printed pp. 154–159.]

pictures.alt: Attendants serve food to travellers in a Chishti khanqah courtyard in medieval Ghiyaspur while devotees gather in the communal hall.
pictures.caption: Chishti hospices joined spiritual teaching with hospitality and food for visitors.

pictures.alt: An ordered Chishti network links Chisht with six teachers and their centres, highlighting Delhi and the deaths in 1325 and 1356.
pictures.caption: Remember the spread of Chishti centres by linking teachers with places.

title: The Chishti Order: Saints, Centres and Public Devotion

body:
The Suhrawardi tradition at Multan

The Suhrawardi silsila developed in the Islamic world around teachers associated with Baghdad, notably Shihab al-Din Umar al-Suhrawardi. In the subcontinent, Bahauddin Zakariya established a major Suhrawardi centre at Multan in the 13th century. Multan is now in Pakistan.

Where prominent Chishti teachers generally preferred distance from political office, the Multan Suhrawardis were more willing to maintain relations with rulers and to retain resources for their institutions. Bahauddin Zakariya had ties with the Delhi Sultan Iltutmish. This is a contrast of general tendencies, not a claim that every Chishti rejected rulers or every Suhrawardi held office.

The other widely named silsilas

The Qadiri order takes its name from Abd al-Qadir Jilani, the 12th-century scholar and preacher associated with Baghdad. The Naqshbandi order takes its name from Bahauddin Naqshband of Bukhara in Central Asia. In Mughal-period India, Baqi Billah was an important early Naqshbandi teacher, followed by his prominent disciple Ahmad Sirhindi, who emphasised adherence to Islamic law and the Prophet's example.

OrderKey associationPlace to remember
ChishtiMuinuddin Chishti; Nizamuddin AuliyaAjmer; Delhi
SuhrawardiShihab al-Din Suhrawardi; Bahauddin ZakariyaBaghdad; Multan
QadiriAbd al-Qadir JilaniBaghdad
NaqshbandiBahauddin Naqshband; Baqi Billah; Ahmad SirhindiBukhara; Mughal India

Regional and unconventional Sufi traditions

The Rishi tradition of Kashmir is associated with Shaikh Nuruddin Wali, also called Nund Rishi, and became influential in Kashmir in the 15th and 16th centuries. Other named lineages included the Shattari order. Separately, wandering groups such as Qalandars and Malangs could follow be-shari'a ascetic practices. These labels should not be confused with the four major silsilas commonly listed in introductory textbooks.

Prelims focus

  • Suhrawardi–Bahauddin Zakariya–Multan; associated with state patronage under the Delhi Sultanate.
  • Qadiri–Abd al-Qadir Jilani–Baghdad.
  • Naqshbandi–Bahauddin Naqshband–Bukhara; Baqi Billah and Ahmad Sirhindi in India.
  • Rishi–Nund Rishi (Nuruddin Wali)–Kashmir.
  • Trap: Bahauddin Zakariya was Suhrawardi, not Chishti.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Class 12, Theme 6, printed pp. 153, 159; NCERT, Our Pasts – II, Class 7, Chapter 8, printed p. 111; GCERT, Social Science, Class 7, Chapter 7, “Bhakti Age: Religious Sects and Saints,” pp. 41–45; Encyclopaedia Iranica, “Khanaqah,” subsection on Suhrawardi hospices (consulted 20 November 2026); Oxford Bibliographies in Islamic Studies, “Abd al-Qadir al Jilani,” Introduction (consulted 20 November 2026); Banglapedia, “Nakshbandia,” introductory article (consulted 20 November 2026).]
